newsitem.title: USA: US Air liable for actual damages in crash.
newsitem.headline: US Air liable for actual damages in crash.

text.p: A federal jury Friday found US Airways Group Inc. at fault in a 1994 crash of a DC-9 jet outside Charlotte, N.C., that claimed 37 lives, but ruled against awarding punitive damages.

The jury had begun deliberating Wednesday evening on whether the airline was liable for the crash of Flight 1016 near Charlotte/Douglas International Airport. It kept up deliberations all day Thursday before issuing its unanimous ruling late Friday morning.

"We were pleased USAir was found responsible. They've denied it from the beginning," said James Orr, a lawyer who represented several relatives of crash victims. "What this is going to do is let airlines know that attorneys representing airline victims are going to stand up and they will take them to trial if necessary."

On July 2, 1994, Flight 1016 was downed by a microburst, a strong downdraft of air that can occur in a thunderstorm and is considered especially dangerous during takeoff and landing, according to aviation authorities' analysis of the accident.
The prosecution had argued during the trial that the aircraft's pilot, Michael Greenlee, should have done more to avoid the thunderstorm.
Defence attorneys had said more of the blame should be borne by air traffic controllers, or the uncontrollable force of nature.
It was not immediately clear what financial impact Friday's ruling would have on US Air. The jury was to return next Wednesday to begin considering the actual damages.
The trial involved 20 consolidated lawsuits filed against the airline in connection with the crash.
Proceedings next week were to address two of those 20 cases. Attorneys said they hoped settlement awards in the first two cases would assist in reaching settlements in the other 18.
Aviation lawyers said such awards typically average about $1 million per case.

During the trial, US Air's lead attorney, Mark Dombroff, had argued that Flight 1016's pilots were not to blame for the crash. To award punitive damages, the jurors would have had to find that the airline caused the crash deliberately or that it acted recklessly.
In the cases of those who died, jurors also could have awarded punitive damages if they decided the airline was grossly negligent.

"For US Air, as with every airline, safety is our top priority," airline spokeswoman Nancy Risque Rohrback said after the jury ruling. However, she said, "I want to emphasise that our sorrow and our sympathy for all those affected by the accident remain constant."
If the jury had decided that the airline was at fault and had awarded punitive damages, it would have been the first U.S. jury to award punitive damages in a commercial aviation case.

Most victims' relatives who attended the trial Friday declined to discuss the ruling. Debra Seymour, whose mother was killed in the crash, expressed some relief. "I'm glad now they have to acknowledge they were at some fault," she said.
